title: Tool Learning Needs Nothing More Than A Free 8B Language Model

paper.title: Tool Learning Needs Nothing More Than A Free 8B Language Model
paper.abstract: Abstract Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a prevalent paradigm for training tool calling agents, which typically requires online interactive environments. Existing approaches either rely on training data with ground truth annotations or require advanced commercial language models (LMs) to synthesize environments that keep fixed once created. In this work, we propose TRUSTEE, a data-free method training tool calling agents with dynamic environments fully simulated by free open-source LMs that can be as small as 8B, including task generation, user simulation, tool simulation and trajectory evaluation, paired with an adaptive curriculum learning mechanism that controls various aspects of the task difficulty dynamically during training. Our empirical results show that TRUSTEE brings consistent improvements across various domains and outperforms all the baselines which require extra external resources for training. These confirm that, with a sufficiently sophisticated design, even simulated environments with a local 8B LM as the backbone could set a strong baseline for tool learning, without expensive annotated data, realistic human interactions, executable tools or costly verifiable environments from human experts or commercial LMs. We hope our proposed paradigm could inspire future research on environment scaling with limited resources.

Existing approaches either rely on training data with ground truth annotations or require advanced commercial language models (LMs) to synthesize environments that keep fixed once created. In this work, we propose TRUSTEE, a data-free method training tool calling agents with dynamic environments fully simulated by free open-source LMs that can be as small as 8B, including task generation, user simulation, tool simulation and trajectory evaluation, paired with an adaptive curriculum learning mechanism that controls various aspects of the task difficulty dynamically during training. Our empirical results show that TRUSTEE brings consistent improvements across various domains and outperforms all the baselines which require extra external resources for training. These confirm that, with a sufficiently sophisticated design, even simulated environments with a local 8B LM as the backbone could set a strong baseline for tool learning, without expensive annotated data, realistic human interactions, executable tools or costly verifiable environments from human experts or commercial LMs. We hope our proposed paradigm could inspire future research on environment scaling with limited resources. 1 Introduction Tool calling, also known as function calling, enables language models (LMs) to interact with the external environment. Thereafter, LMs have become active agents that can have access to external information Zhuang et al. (2023) , make use of realistic services Patil et al. (2024) ; Schick et al. (2023) , and even make changes to the world Yao et al. (2023) . With the prevalence of agentic reinforcement learning (agentic RL) Jin et al. (2025) , more and more work has been focusing on teaching LMs to call tools ( i.e. , tool learning) via RL. Earlier work directly adopt data for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), which requires ground truth annotations, for single-turn reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) Qian et al. (2025a) ; Zhang et al. (2025b) ; Zeng et al. (2025) . However, due to the cost and limited availability of real-world tools and users, when it comes to truly online multi-turn RL, there is a significant challenge in scaling the environment 1 1 1 In this paper, environment refers to all the external components for the agent, including users, tools and other entities like an optional verifier. , for that such kind of RL requires a large number of online interactions including calling many tools and dynamically interacting with the user, which has also challenged evaluation Ruan et al. (2024) ; Guo et al. (2024) and SFT data construction Fang et al. (2025) ; Chen et al. (2025) ; Liu et al. (2025) . One approach of environment scaling is to apply LMs but most of these work only partially simulates the environment (simulates either the tools Sullivan et al. (2025) ; Castellani et al. (2025) ; Li et al. (2026) or the users Qian et al. (2025b) ) and relies on existing data or environments ( i.e. , supports some specific tasks only). For instance, Simia-RL Li et al. (2025) simulates the responses of tools with LMs during interactions, but requires established data containing training tasks as the input ( e.g. , τ \tau -bench Yao et al. (2025) ) and does not support the multi-turn interaction between the agent and the user. Another approach is to make use of synthesized code and databases Song et al. (2026) ; Wang et al. (2026) , but such approach requires a complex generation pipeline for high-quality synthesis using expensive commercial LMs and the generated environments and tasks are fixed once created, which may be too easy for strong agents but overly difficult for weak ones. To this end, we introduce TRUSTEE, T ool lea R ning U sing S imula TE d E nvironments, a data-free method training tool calling agents with a local open-source LM as the only required resource. TRUSTEE uses an LM to generate the task, simulate the user, simulate tool responses, and evaluate the trajectories, which provides complete environments for tool learning while independent of any existing training data or tasks, human annotations or interactions, realistic executable tools, or verifiable environments engineered by experts or commercial LMs. Moreover, we design an A daptive C urriculum L earning (ACL) mechanism that takes the advantage of the dynamically controllable nature of the simulated environments and tasks, which controls the difficulty of the tasks in various aspects based on the reward of the last step adaptively and ensures a smooth learning process for the tool calling agent. Our empirical evaluation validates the effectiveness of TRUSTEE. The Qwen3-8B LM, when trained solely with environments simulated by itself, outperforms all the baselines which either require annotated data or need advanced commercial LMs to synthesize or instantiate the environments. This proves that, with sufficiently sophisticated designs, simulated environments may serve as a powerful approach to tool learning that can even beat realistic data or synthesized verifiable environments. Our contributions include: • We introduce TRUSTEE, a paradigm of simulating every environment component with an LM for RL-based tool learning, paired with adaptive curriculum learning that dynamically keeps the tasks and environments at an appropriate difficulty for the agent. • We run computational experiments and demonstrate the effectiveness of TRUSTEE, confirming even a fully simulated environment with an 8B open-source LM can lead to a competitive tool calling agent. • We validate that tool learning does not necessarily require established data, realistic human interactions, executable tools, and verifiable environments from human experts or commercial LMs, moving a step towards cost-friendly tool learning. Our code will be publicly available when this work is completely finished. 2 Method 2.1 Problem Formulation We formalize the tool calling agent task as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) Zhang et al.
